Messages.Author: PDB6
Messages.Body:
Robert Frankiln Grau wrote:
"I think Eric has summarized the issue well. I remember the debate
surrounding Ian Forestal right after the Sabbat expansion came out in 1996.
There were similar comments about how his ability was way overpowered for an 8
cap vamp, and how the Tremere were going to be unstoppable after Sabbat, yada,
yada, yada."

As a very vocal part of that original Ian Forrestal argument, I would say that
the problem with him (and the argument at the time) was not that he was too
powerful and would destroy game balance, but that he was a complete slap in the
face to the original vampire design system and a sign of bad things to come,
which he was. The vampires in the Sabbat set were designed seemingly
completely randomly when compared to the original set vamps. 4 point vampires
with 5 points of abilites. 6 point vampires with 8 points of abilities. 7
point vampires with 4 points of abilities. 8 point vampires with 20 points of
abilites. It was just not good.

Ian Forrestal is not too powerful on a grand scheme. However, he is just
completely wrong when compared to similarly sized vampires. As far as I
remember, he has 6 points of disciplines, and then every other discipline in
the game at inferior. This is completely preposterous from a design
standpoint, as all other vampires were required to pay for all of their
inferior disciplines. Whay should Ian get them all for free? Becasue it is a
special ability? That is just dumb.

Peter D Bakija

Messages.Author: PDB6
Messages.Body:
Eric Petterson wrote:
"Hmm, as a participant on the opposite side of that debate, I remember the
words "overpowered" and "broken" being thrown around. :-)"

Well, he is clearly "broken" and in a sense "overpowered", but not in a way
that will destroy the game environment on a practical level.

"My argument, as I recall, was that in order to get "your money's worth" from
Ian's inferiors, you would have to use a deck with so many disciplines that it
could never be very effective."

And that same argument can hold for every large vampire in the game, yet they
all have to pay for their extra disciplines, in terms of larger capacity. Take
Democritus for instance. You are never, in one deck, going to use PRE, DOM,
for, aus, and cel, yet Democritus has to be a 10 to justify having all of these
disciplines. If, for instance, he didn't have the fairly useless aus, he could
possibly have FOR (and thus at least be an effective Ventrue) for the same
cost. In order to get your money's worth from any vampire with 4 or more
disciplines, you have to use a deck with so many disciplines it could never be
effective. However, all of these vampires pay for each and every discipline
they have, where Ian does not. He is getting an awful lot of stuff for free.

"I think time has shown that Ian is not overpowered."

Does he break the game? No, in a similar way to Dreams of the Sphinx. Dreams
does not break the game, yet Dreams is pretty widely regarded as a card that is
too good and should not have been introduced into the set. Same with Jimmy
Dunn. Ian is completely wrong, just like Dreams and Jimmy, and should not have
been made.

"I personally see no reason that the vampire "formula" can't be ignored if the
result is a well-balanced vampire."

But balance only exisits in the context of what it is balanced against. The
Sabbat set completely threw the vampire formula completely out the window, and
ended up with vampires like Sela, Sheila Mezzarin, and Jessica, that when
compared to their fairly similar Camarilla counterparts, are much more
powereful for the same cost.

"Now, the Sabbat expansion has vampires that are both too good for their cost
and too weak, because they varied from the "formula" without proper balancing
abilities/penalties. Sela is too good. Most of the !Gangrel are too weak. ;-)
Ian, however, is fine."

The Sabbat set vampires were a unholy nightmare. Again, however, because of
the way the game works, and everyone can benefit from the bustedness at the
same time, it doesn't have that much of an effect on the game (other than
relegating many Camrilla vampires to the "obsolete" pile). However, I belive
that the game would have benefitted far more from the set if the vamps had been
designed using the same rules as the basic set vamps.

>This is completely preposterous from a design
>standpoint, as all other vampires were required to pay for all of their
>inferior disciplines. Whay should Ian get them all for free? Becasue it is a
>special ability?

Technically, yes, Ian does get them all for free. But look at it from
another point of view. How many decks do you play with more than, say,
three disciplines in it? Though technically Ian could play any
discipline card you had in your deck, you restrict his ability by not
having those cards for him to play.

If it was a very esoteric discipline combination, I might not mind
paying 8 blood for a vampire with all three at inferior but I would
generally not put Ian in a deck unless one of his superior disciplines
was involved. In that case, his other two points are the two other
disciplines I was playing - maybe cel, THA, obf or something like
(maybe, rush combat, blurred Thefts and a little bit of stealth or
something, I dunno). The only real thing with Ian is that his
disciplines would then "change" between each deck I put him in. And for
an 8 capacity vampire, that isn't too bad anyway.

Of course, I could see hideousness going on with him if you team up with
someone using a Succubus Club but that's another story entirely....

focus issues. Consider if Masika had six inferior disciplines instead of
three superior disciplines -- would he be as good? The answer is no.

I think later expansions tried to give larger vampires "more stuff" because
"the formula" was overcharging them for disciplines. The result has been
haphazard, but I understand the motivation.

Messages.Author: Chris Berger
Messages.Body:
>
> Eric Petterson wrote:
> "Hmm, as a participant on the opposite side of that debate, I remember the
> words "overpowered" and "broken" being thrown around. :-)"
>
> Well, he is clearly "broken" and in a sense "overpowered", but not in a way
> that will destroy the game environment on a practical level.
>

Bah! "Broken" or "overpowered" mean that a card is more useful than any
other cards with comparable cost. Ian is not. He's overpriced in a
"standard" 3 discipline Tremere deck. He's only useful if you build a
deck to take advantage of him, just like Powerbases are "overpowered"
compared to Investments if you build a deck to take advantage of them.

>
> "I think time has shown that Ian is not overpowered."
>
> Does he break the game? No, in a similar way to Dreams of the Sphinx. Dreams
> does not break the game, yet Dreams is pretty widely regarded as a card that is

> too good and should not have been introduced into the set. Same with Jimmy

> Dunn. Ian is completely wrong, just like Dreams and Jimmy, and should not have
> been made.
>
Bah, again! Ian isn't wrong at all. He simply has a special ability (a
5 point special, at that), that allows him to pretend he has all of the
disciplines. IMNSHO, 5 points is a perfect price to pay for that
special, as even 5 disciplines are an awful lot to use in one deck.
Just think, if you use a 5 discipline deck, then IAN operates by the
normal vampire formula. How many 5 discipline decks do you use? Then,
his 3 superiors are simply 1 point each, because they are added to his
special ability of having everything at inferior.

What your debating is not whether he fits the vampire formula, but
whether his special is worth 5 points. How many do you think it should
be worth? This discount for quantity is not unprecedented in other
areas, so why should it be so "wrong" in Jyhad?

-Chris

Why five points?

Card Title: Ian Forestal
Capacity: 8
Disciplines: THA AUS DOM
Clan: Tremere Antitribu
Card Text: Sabbat: Ian can play cards of any Discipline as though
he has the basic level of that Discipline. Master
Discipline cards played on him grant the superior level
of that Discipline.

6 points of disciplines, 8 capacity vampire. Taking him, therefore, as
either 8 or 9 (I can never remember if it's 8 and above or above 8 for
adding an extra point to the vamp), that's still only 2 or 3 points for
his ability.

However, I do agree with you. He is versatile enough to go into any
deck, of course, but expensive enough to put you off doing it. I mean,
I see plenty of decks with Dreams in them, but how many have I ever seen
with Ian Forestal in?

Messages.Author: PDB6
Messages.Body:
RYOGAtheH wrote:
"he's fine... they are all fine quit whining and use them yourself =D"

Yeah, that's helpful. What you seem to be missing out on is that most
arguments around here come from one of two highly divergent viewpoints:

A) That Jyhad was designed as a well balanced game with appropriate cost for
comparable ability to be the very basis of the game. People who believe this
to be the case are generally very critical of cards that ignore this balance
and find such cards to be damaging to the game as whole.

B) That Jyhad is a card game, so super powered Rares and random throwing out of
balance is all part and parcel of the genre, and as such, is perfecly
acceptable. Besides, there is always Sudden Reversal or Direct Intervention.

Clearly, I always argue from the standpoint of (A), while most new posters tend
to argue from the (B) standpoint. I'm not quite sure why that is.

Messages.Author: The Corrupter
Messages.Body:
On 19 Jul 1998, RYOGAtheH wrote:

> he's fine... they are all fine quit whining and use them yourself =D

Well, that's a no...

First, to whining.

It seems that the last stand of the person who has no intelligent point
to make is "quit your whining".
Why is that?
Well, the primary reason is likely, since these people have a lack of
pointed, reasonable arguments to make, they are going to try to shame
their opponents from speaking. Unconsciously (sp?), they know that their
argument is lacking in reason, and one of the only ways to disarm an
intelligent opponent is cause their response to be inflamed (the insult)
or silenced (fear of mockery, etc).

---
Why am I going off on this?

I've grown sick, of late, of people's complaints about play balance, game
support, card pool, and other issues (both in this game and in the Other
game) being dismissed by the complacent and slow-minded as whining. I've
been annoyed at people agreeing with me on the non-issue of a certain
topic by calling that person "a whiner".

Maybe they are right. Maybe they are wrong. And maybe they are
whining. But, I'll be damned if you're going to waste my time and my
bandwith by declaring someone a whiner. If you disagree, convince them,
argue with them, debate with them. Leave the name-calling on the playground.

-whining

There are two points of view: that there IS a problem with game balance
[your view] and that there is not [my view]. In principle, these two
points of view could be tested scientifically, by looking at the decks
that win and proving that one discipline, clan or strategy was so absurdly
dominant that the others didn't have a chance. That data has not been
collected, so right now both points of view are valid. Clearly our
subjective impressions of the existing situation are different, otherwise
we would not disagree.

And i'm sorry if you are offended by being called [though not by me] a
whiner. Fortunately i have a much thicker skin than you, and don't in the
slightest resent the implication that i am slow-minded and complacent.

Also, I'd like to add that the CL/NL-issue is also responsible for the
diverging opinions on the "brokenness" of cards. While in NL, cards
appear often, they don't do as often with CL. Therefore, many CL players
don't think of these powercards as broken, because they do not dominate
the game.

I play CL myself. In my environment, I don't think that the discussed
cards are such a huge problem. A bit nasty perhaps, but that's all.
But I can clearly understand that in NL, they pose a serious problem.

And no, the existance of a counter card (namely DI, SR) doesn't justify
the existence of such powerful cards.

Yet again, this does not mean that powerful cards have to be completely
re-written. Minor changes can be enough to soften the effects of these
cards. Take Fame: the Methuselah takes the pool loss, whose turn it
actually is. Or Tomb: for each blood transferred to the vamp, add a
-1 capacity/blood counter to that vamp. (after the vamp is controlled, these
counters could be burned or not.)
Zip Gun: is not a gun, only weapon.

You see, there are possibilities to make changes without making the
cards function totally different.

I agree with most other players, that the problem cards are too powerful,
but I doubt that rewording or banning will do any good.

-Carl

And, in thinking about what if anything needs fixing we need to remember
that competitive play is only a tiny, minor aspect of Jyhad. It bears the
same relationship to real Jyhad as the one-night stand does to marriage,
and you will get into serious trouble if you apply the same rules to your
marriage as you do in your affaires.

impact on the tournament scene here, but that us because it is relatively
young.

I think we can all agree that the only area of Jyhad in which the
"problem" cards MAY be a problem is competitive play. Personally I do not
regard competitive play as the motor of this game.

blue? -- "no, it's rather grey this morning..." -- SMACK!!).

They are also a problem when you play some smart-aleck kid at the local game
store. Or when your so-called friends refuse to see that their Mind Rape-RtI
deck and their Anarch vote deck don't make them better players than you. My
problem has always been that if you don't play competitively, what's the
point? The point of the game is to try and win. If you have to shame people
out of playing to win, then there's not much point to the game. Okay, I
suppose you can always applaud the person who wins with a Wolf Companion
deck, or with a pot-tha deck, but you also know they'd get stomped by any
deck with a few broken cards in it. And then you get problems with stuff
like PF. If you're playing Fortitude or Potence, you're almost stupid not to
put it in. But are people going to call your deck broken if you put just a
few in? And how many is too many? I prefer things cut and dried... I want
everyone to be able to play whatever they want, and the better player still
at least has a chance of winning (the better player doesn't have to *always*
win... that might also get boring).

So yeah, the power cards are the most problematic in a tournament game, but
they can be annoying and stupid even when playing casual games.

if it could, you'd end up with every deck having: guns, bleed bounce/AI, tons

tournaments(at least, every one that I've ever been at)? They have S:CE,
damage prevention, untap, bleed, vote, titles, what have you. But since, in

never meta-gamed away (and as I said above, I don't think even this could get

Well then we may be even closer than I thought. As far as the "major"
re-writes go (I include Mind Rape, Return to Innocence, and Tomb of Ramses
III), I disagree on them and think that smaller changes would be in order and
might actually get more support. I've tried to keep from saying that too
much, since it would undermine the main point I was trying to make (which is
that, in general, LSJ has done a *great* job with the new rulings, and that
those cards *needed* to be changed). As for the other changes, many of them
were "non-errata" such as Rotchreck, (D) actions, combat card duration (i.e.
Immortal Grapple), and damage prevention (can be used anytime during combat).
Others, like the Rutor's Hand errata, and the no-(D) bleeds, were made just
to keep things in line with the errata and rulings that no longer existed.
These, in fact, make the game *more* accessible, by causing it to work more
as the rule book and cards (and common sense) would imply. In fact, I really
think that the only thing that makes it less-accessible are the rewrites, all
of which, I still maintain, were necessary (well, WwEF might have been
unnecessary, but it's a really minor thing... hardly a rewrite).

As for the pushes to errata more cards... there are really only a few out
there, and I don't think it will ever degenerate to the free-for-all
errata-fest you are envisioning. Personally, I think all of the broken cards
have been fixed. Protected Resources, Archon Investigation, and Direct
Intervention are not, IMO, broken. There's really very little to compare
them to to say that they are undercosted. Protected Resources only *really*
hurts RtI, which has been fixed, and it pretty much hurts bruise & bleed... I
think bruise and bleed can work around this, and might post a message about
it later (actually, I'd like to write an entire post about B&B decks).
Archon Investigation punishes the nasty stealth bleeder, while also hurting
bruise and bleed. I don't particularly like the card, but more often than
not it just sits in your hand. Direct Intervention is similar in power to
Sudden Reversal, if not weaker. I just plain don't like the card, but then,
I never liked SR either. Counterspells suck big time, but that's not a valid
reason for errata-ing or banning the card. I could see banning those 3 cards
(or maybe just PR and AI) in tournament play, but in general they're not ban
or change material as is. Anything else that's up for weakening (e.g. Hostile
Takeover) is rather silly.
